name.text: 01 Content: Why a Version Control System Belongs in a Philology Course

questiontext.text:
Why a Version Control System Belongs in a Philology Course

You have enrolled in a course about historical documents, and the first thing you will be asked to learn is a piece of software written for programmers. That sequence deserves an explanation, because the justification is not that Git is a useful job skill — though it is — but that Git is a formal model of the very thing textual criticism has always studied.

Textual criticism exists because texts change as they are copied. A scribe working from an exemplar introduces errors, corrections, and deliberate alterations; a later scribe copies that copy, inheriting some changes and adding others. The discipline's central problem is reconstructing the relationships among those states from the surviving evidence. Git exists because software changes as it is edited, and its central problem is recording the relationships among those states exactly. The two disciplines converged on the same abstract structure independently, and the convergence is not a coincidence: both are concerned with tracking variant states of a document across a branching history of transmission.

Huskey (2024) makes this argument directly, proposing that scholarly editors treat the Git repository as a research journal rather than as file storage. The claim is stronger than it sounds. A research journal is not a backup; it is an argument in progress, in which each entry is dated, attributed, and justified. A Git repository used properly has exactly those properties, and a Git repository used carelessly has none of them. The difference lies entirely in the discipline of the person committing.

Vocabulary. Version control system (VCS) — software that records the state of a set of files at successive points in time, with the metadata needed to identify, compare, and recover any of those states. Exemplar — the manuscript a scribe copies from. Witness — any surviving manuscript that attests a text.

Takeaway: Git is on the syllabus because its data model formalizes textual transmission, not because digital humanists are expected to know developer tools.

name.text: 02 Content: The Print Edition as a Lossy Record: Giarratano's *Bucolica*

questiontext.text:
The Print Edition as a Lossy Record: Giarratano's *Bucolica*

The best case for version-controlled editing is a case where its absence destroyed evidence. Huskey (2024) analyzes the editorial career of Caesar Giarratano, who published five separate print editions of Calpurnius Siculus' Bucolica between 1910 and 1951 — five editions of the same short pastoral text, by the same editor, across forty-one years.

Across those editions Giarratano changed his method fundamentally. He moved from a positive critical apparatus, which records all variant readings including the one printed in the text, to a negative apparatus, which records only the readings rejected. He abandoned his Greek-character manuscript sigla in favour of Latin characters, silently renaming every witness in the edition. These are not typographical adjustments; they are systemic changes to how the edition represents evidence, and each implies a changed view of what an apparatus is for (Huskey, 2024).

The rationale for those changes is gone. Print editions record outcomes, not reasoning: the reader receives the finished apparatus with no account of why its form changed between 1910 and 1951. A scholar today who wants to understand Giarratano's development must physically obtain all five volumes and collate them by hand — performing textual criticism on a modern critical edition, which is precisely the labour the edition was supposed to spare them (Huskey, 2024).

Had Giarratano worked in a version-controlled repository, the change of sigla would have been a single documented commit with a stated reason, and the shift from positive to negative apparatus would have been a documented restructuring. The evidence would still exist. This is the concrete stake of the discipline you are about to learn: what is not committed with rationale is not recoverable.

Takeaway: Print editions preserve the editor's conclusions and discard the editor's reasoning; a version-controlled edition preserves both.

name.text: 03 Content: The Critical Apparatus and the Commit Log Are the Same Object

questiontext.text:
The Critical Apparatus and the Commit Log Are the Same Object

Consider what a critical apparatus does. Against a base text, it records alternative readings, each attributed to a witness, each located at a precise point in the text. It is a structured record of deviation from a reference state.

Now consider what git log combined with git diff does. Against a base state, it records alternative states, each attributed to an author, each located at a precise point in the file. The structural correspondence is exact, and Huskey (2024) argues it should be exploited pedagogically rather than treated as a curiosity.

The correspondence extends through the whole vocabulary of the discipline, which is why this course can teach both at once:

Philological concept Git equivalent Shared epistemological function
Exemplar or archetype The main branch The reference state from which variants deviate
Scribal copying git clone, git branch Duplicating a text so it can be altered independently
Variant reading or emendation git commit A dated, attributed alteration with stated rationale
Critical apparatus git diff, git log The aggregated record of deviation from the reference
Stemma codicum The commit graph The genealogy of states and their descent relations
Siglum Commit hash A short unique label identifying one witness or state

There is one important asymmetry. The scribe did not intend to create an apparatus; the apparatus is reconstructed after the fact by an editor working from damaged and partial evidence. You, by contrast, are generating your own transmission history deliberately and in full. You are in the unusual position of being both the scribe and the editor of your own text — which means the quality of your apparatus is entirely within your control, and entirely your responsibility.

Takeaway: You will produce two editions this term: the TEI edition of your passage, and the Git history that documents how you arrived at it.

name.text: 04 Content: Content-Addressable Storage: What Git Actually Stores

questiontext.text:
Content-Addressable Storage: What Git Actually Stores

Most people's mental model of version control is that it stores a list of changes — a file, then a patch, then another patch. That model is wrong for Git, and holding it will make Git's behaviour seem arbitrary. Git stores complete snapshots, and it addresses them by their content.

A content-addressable store is one in which an object's name is derived from its contents rather than assigned externally. Git computes a SHA-1 checksum over each object's bytes, producing a forty-character hexadecimal identifier, and that identifier is the object's name in the database (Chacon & Straub, 2014). The consequence is that identical content necessarily has an identical name: if two of your transcription files contain exactly the same text, Git stores that content once and points at it twice, whatever the files are called and wherever they sit in the directory tree.

The philological payoff is immediate. Because the name is derived from the content, the name cannot disagree with the content. If a byte changes, the hash changes; if the hash is unchanged, no byte has changed. There is no way to alter a stored transcription while leaving its identifier intact, which means the identifier functions as a tamper-evident seal on the state of your edition at a moment in time (Chacon & Straub, 2014).

This is why Git can make guarantees that a folder of files named transcription_v2_FINAL_revised.xml cannot. Manual versioning schemes encode your intentions in filenames, and filenames lie — they are assigned by a tired student at midnight and are not checked against anything. Hashes are computed from the data and cannot lie.

Vocabulary. SHA-1 — a cryptographic hash function producing a 160-bit (40 hex character) digest. Checksum — a value computed from data such that a change in the data changes the value. Content-addressable — named by content rather than by assigned label.

Takeaway: Git names every stored object by a hash of its contents, so an object's identifier is a verifiable claim about its bytes.

name.text: 05 Content: The Four Object Types: Blobs, Trees, Commits, and Tags

questiontext.text:
The Four Object Types: Blobs, Trees, Commits, and Tags

The entire Git database is built from four object types. Understanding them is not optional trivia; nearly every confusing Git behaviour you will encounter this term becomes obvious once you know which object is involved.

A blob stores the raw contents of a file, and nothing else — no filename, no path, no timestamp, no permissions. A blob of your transcription is just the bytes of the transcription. A tree supplies exactly what the blob omits: it is a directory listing, mapping names to the hashes of blobs and of other trees, along with file mode information. A commit points to a single root tree — that is, to a complete snapshot of the project — and adds the metadata that makes the snapshot meaningful: author, committer, timestamp, message, and pointers to its parent commit or commits. A tag is a named, optionally signed pointer to a specific commit, used to mark states that matter permanently (Chacon & Straub, 2014).

Object Stores Points to Editorial analogue
Blob Raw file contents Nothing The text of one witness, unlabelled
Tree Names, modes, structure Blobs and sub-trees The physical arrangement of a codex
Commit Author, date, message One root tree, parent commits A dated editorial intervention with rationale
Tag A label, optionally signed One commit A published edition, cited by version

The separation of blob from tree explains a behaviour that puzzles new users: Git does not track file renames as such. When you rename a transcription file, the blob is unchanged — the content did not change — and only the tree entry differs. Git detects renames after the fact by noticing that a blob left one path and arrived at another, rather than by recording a rename operation.

Takeaway: Blobs hold content, trees hold structure, commits hold history and rationale, and tags mark states worth citing.

name.text: 06 Content: The Directed Acyclic Graph

questiontext.text:
The Directed Acyclic Graph

Because every commit stores the hash of its parent, commits chain backwards through time. That chain is not a simple line: a commit may have two parents (a merge), and several commits may share one parent (a branch point). The resulting structure is a directed acyclic graph, or DAG (Chacon & Straub, 2014).

Each word in the term does work. Directed: the parent relation has an orientation — a commit knows its parents, but a parent does not know its children, exactly as an exemplar does not know what was copied from it. Acyclic: there are no loops, because a commit's hash incorporates its parents' hashes, so a commit cannot be its own ancestor. Graph: the structure is a network of nodes and edges, not a list.

The philological reader will recognize this shape immediately. A stemma codicum is a directed acyclic graph over manuscripts: descent has an orientation, no manuscript descends from itself, and the structure branches. The two fields arrived at the same formalism because they are modelling the same phenomenon — descent with modification through copying (Huskey, 2024).

There is one instructive place where the analogy breaks, and it is worth noticing now. Stemmatic reconstruction is inference under uncertainty: the editor infers relations among witnesses from shared errors, because the actual history is unobserved and most intermediate copies are lost. Your Git DAG, by contrast, is observed — it is not reconstructed but recorded, complete, with no missing intermediaries. This term you will experience what a philologist almost never has: a transmission history with no gaps in it.

Vocabulary. DAG — a set of nodes connected by directed edges containing no cycles. Stemma codicum — the genealogical tree of a text's surviving witnesses. Merge commit — a commit with more than one parent.

Takeaway: A repository's history is a directed acyclic graph, the same formal structure as a stemma — but recorded rather than inferred.

answer.text: A commit's hash incorporates its parents' hashes, so a commit cannot be its own ancestor.

feedback.text: Correct. Acyclicity is enforced mathematically by the hashing scheme rather than by a rule.

name.text: 07 Content: Cryptographic Integrity and the Cascading Hash

questiontext.text:
Cryptographic Integrity and the Cascading Hash

The properties described so far combine into something stronger than either alone. Because a commit's hash is computed over its content — which includes its tree hash and its parent hashes — a change anywhere in the history propagates outward to every commit that descends from it.

Follow the cascade concretely. You alter a single combining diacritic in a TEI transcription. The file's bytes differ, so its blob hash differs. The tree listing that blob now references a different hash, so the tree's own hash differs. The commit pointing at that tree now references a different tree hash, so the commit hash differs. Every subsequent commit references a changed parent hash, so every one of them changes too (Chacon & Straub, 2014).

The security consequence is that silent tampering is not merely difficult but structurally impossible. There is no way to reach into the middle of a repository's history, alter a reading, and leave the surrounding history intact: either the downstream hashes change and the alteration is visible, or they do not change and the alteration did not happen. History can be rewritten — Git provides tools for that — but a rewrite produces a visibly different graph. It cannot be done invisibly.

For a scholarly edition this is the guarantee that matters. Huskey's (2024) argument for reproducibility and explainability in editing depends on the audit trail being trustworthy; an audit trail that could be quietly edited afterwards would establish nothing. The cryptographic chain is what converts "here is my work log" into "here is a verifiable claim about my work."

Takeaway: A change anywhere in history changes every hash downstream of it, so a repository's history cannot be altered without leaving evidence.

name.text: 08 Content: Branching, and Why You Will Use It for Editorial Hypotheses

questiontext.text:
Branching, and Why You Will Use It for Editorial Hypotheses

A branch in Git is startlingly cheap: it is a file containing a single commit hash, plus a name. Creating one costs a few dozen bytes, which is why Git encourages branching in situations where older version control systems made it a significant undertaking (Chacon & Straub, 2014).

The editorial use is the interesting one. You will frequently face a decision with no clearly correct answer: whether to treat a marginal addition as part of the text or as apparatus, whether a damaged sequence is best restored one way or another, whether to encode a correction with <sic>/<corr> or to leave it diplomatic. The traditional response is to choose, proceed, and record the rejected option in a footnote. The version-controlled response is to encode both fully, on separate branches, and compare the finished results before deciding.

This changes what an editorial hypothesis costs. On paper, pursuing an alternative encoding through an entire passage is expensive enough that editors rarely do it, and so alternatives are usually rejected on the basis of a prospective judgement rather than a completed trial. On a branch, the same experiment costs almost nothing and can be abandoned without trace or merged without penalty. You should expect to use this repeatedly from Week 6 onward, when normalization decisions start to have consequences that only become visible several steps later in the pipeline.

The Perseids Platform makes exactly this affordance central to its pedagogy: students work on their own branches precisely so that they can attempt difficult encoding without risking the shared text, and submit the result for editorial review only once it is complete (Almas & Beaulieu, 2012).

Takeaway: Branches make editorial alternatives cheap enough to test rather than merely to speculate about.

name.text: 09 Content: Installing Git and Declaring Who You Are

questiontext.text:
Installing Git and Declaring Who You Are

Before the first commit, Git needs to know how to attribute your work. This is not a formality: authorship metadata is baked into every commit object and cannot be changed later without rewriting history.

Configure your identity globally, once, on each machine you will work on:

git config --global user.name "Your Full Name"
git config --global user.email "yourid@stfx.ca"

Use the name you want to appear in the permanent record of your edition, in the form you would use in a publication. Use your StFX address rather than a personal one, since the repository will be reviewed as coursework. If you also work on a personal laptop, configure it identically — commits made under two different identities look like two different editors to anyone reading the log later, and the resulting apparatus is misattributed.

Two further global settings will save you difficulty in Week 4 and after. Set the default branch name explicitly, and set your editor to something you can actually exit:

Setting Command Why it matters here
Default branch name git config --global init.defaultBranch main Keeps every student repository consistent for review
Commit editor git config --global core.editor "code --wait" Enables multi-line commit bodies without vi
Rebase on pull git config --global pull.rebase false Preserves merge commits as evidence of integration

Verify the result with git config --global --list before continuing. Everything in this course accumulates, and an identity error committed today propagates through every assignment that follows.

Takeaway: Authorship metadata is permanent in the commit object, so configure it correctly before the first commit rather than after.

name.text: 10 Content: Initializing the Repository for Your Edition

questiontext.text:
Initializing the Repository for Your Edition

Each of you will maintain a single repository for the whole term, containing the passage you select this week and every layer of encoding you subsequently build on it. Create it now, in a location you will not lose:

mkdir rels398-edition
cd rels398-edition
git init

git init creates a .git directory. That hidden directory is the repository: the object database, the references, the configuration, and the hooks all live inside it. The visible files beside it are merely the currently checked-out state — a view of one commit, which Git can regenerate at any time from the objects it holds. Deleting .git deletes your entire history while leaving the current files intact, which is a mistake that looks harmless right up until you need an earlier state.

Establish the directory structure now rather than reorganizing later. The layout below mirrors the distinction between source material, working files, and outputs that the course assignments assume:

Directory Holds Populated in
images/ Facsimile images and IIIF manifest for your passage Week 3
transcription/ Diplomatic and normalized transcriptions Weeks 4–6
collation/ Witness files, CollateX input and output Week 7
edition/ The TEI file with apparatus, lemmatization, commentary Weeks 8–12
logs/ Error-rate reports, AI-usage notes, reconciliation records Weeks 5 onward

Add a README.md at the root stating which manuscript passage you have chosen and why. That file is the first thing a reviewer reads, and by the end of term it will be the front matter of your edition.

Takeaway: .git is the repository and the visible files are just a checked-out view of it; structure the working tree once, at the start.

name.text: 11 Content: The Three States: Working Directory, Staging Area, Repository

questiontext.text:
The Three States: Working Directory, Staging Area, Repository

Git's most distinctive feature, and the one that most reliably confuses newcomers, is that a file exists in three places at once. Understanding the three states is what makes atomic committing possible.

The working directory is what you see and edit: ordinary files on disk. The staging area — also called the index — is a proposed next commit, holding the exact content that will be recorded when you commit. The repository is the object database in .git, holding every committed state permanently (Chacon & Straub, 2014).

State Contents Moved into it by Reverted by
Working directory Files as currently edited Editing in Oxygen or VS Code git restore <file>
Staging area The proposed next commit git add <file> git restore --staged <file>
Repository All permanently recorded states git commit git revert <commit>

The staging area is what separates Git from a backup tool, and it exists precisely so that what you commit need not be everything you have changed. In a morning's work you may fix a typographic error in a transcription, adjust the TEI header, and experiment with an encoding you are not yet sure about. Those are three different scholarly acts. The staging area lets you record them as three commits, in an order you choose, rather than as one undifferentiated lump.

Use git status constantly — it reports which files sit in which state, and it suggests the command to move them. Experienced users run it more often than any other command, not less.

Takeaway: The staging area exists so that a commit can record one logical change rather than everything you happen to have edited.

name.text: 12 Content: Your First Commit

questiontext.text:
Your First Commit

With the structure in place, record the initial state. The sequence is: inspect, stage, inspect again, commit.

git status
git add README.md
git status
git commit -m "chore(repo): initialize edition repository with README"

Note the deliberate second git status. Staging is the step where mistakes happen — a stray file, a forgotten file, an editor backup — and it is far easier to correct the index before committing than to correct the history afterwards. Read what Git tells you is staged, and confirm it is what you meant.

The -m flag supplies a single-line message. It is convenient and it is the right tool for a genuinely trivial commit, but it will not serve you for most of this term's work, because a one-line message cannot carry rationale. From Week 4 onward, run git commit with no -m, let your editor open, and write a subject line followed by a blank line and a body explaining why.

A frequent early error deserves naming: git add . stages everything in the directory, including files you did not intend to track — editor swap files, operating system metadata, large image derivatives, and half-finished experiments. Prefer naming files explicitly. Where a broad add is genuinely convenient, protect yourself first with a .gitignore file listing the patterns that should never be tracked, such as .DS_Store, *~, and .vscode/.

Takeaway: Stage deliberately and inspect the index before committing; correcting the staging area is trivial, correcting history is not.

name.text: 13 Content: Atomic Commits as Cognitive Discipline

questiontext.text:
Atomic Commits as Cognitive Discipline

An atomic commit records exactly one logical change — one scholarly act, complete in itself. The requirement sounds like tidiness. It is in fact the central intellectual discipline of this course's version control practice, and Huskey (2024) treats it as the precondition for a repository functioning as a research journal at all.

Consider why. If a commit contains one change, its message can state what that change was and why it was made, and the message is verifiable against the diff. If a commit contains six unrelated changes, no honest message can describe it — the author is forced into vagueness ("various corrections"), and the record becomes unusable for exactly the purpose it was created to serve. Non-atomic commits do not merely make history untidy; they make it uninformative.

Atomicity also determines whether history is reversible. Suppose you later discover that your treatment of a particular abbreviation was wrong. If that decision was applied in its own commit, you can revert precisely it, leaving everything else untouched. If it was bundled with your header metadata and three transcription corrections, reverting it means losing those too, and you will instead redo the work by hand — which is to say the history provided no protection at all.

The practical test is a sentence. Before committing, state what the commit does in one clause without using "and". "Corrects the iotacism at line 14." "Adds the TEI header." If you need "and", or if you find yourself reaching for a semicolon, you are looking at two commits.

Vocabulary. Atomic commit — a commit recording a single logical change that is complete and independently reversible. Revert — a new commit that undoes the effect of an earlier one, without erasing it from history.

Takeaway: If you cannot describe a commit in one clause without "and", it is more than one commit.

name.text: 14 Content: What Non-Atomic Commits Look Like in Practice

questiontext.text:
What Non-Atomic Commits Look Like in Practice

Recognizing the failure is easier than defining the rule. The table below contrasts commits from a real editorial workflow — the left column shows patterns that recur constantly in student repositories, the right shows the same work recorded usably.

Non-atomic commit Why it fails Atomic replacement
updates Describes nothing; diff must be read to learn anything Separate commits, each naming its change
fixed typos and added header Two unrelated acts; neither is separately reversible fix(transcription): correct itacism at 3.14, then feat(header): add teiHeader
end of day Groups by time rather than by meaning One commit per decision made that day
AI stuff Hides provenance of machine-generated content feat(transcription): add LLM draft with an AI-Generated: true trailer
asdfasdf Placeholder committed in haste and never revisited Any message stating the actual change

Two habits produce most non-atomic commits. The first is committing by clock rather than by meaning — working for three hours and then committing whatever has accumulated. The remedy is to commit when a change is finished, not when you stop working. The second is treating commits as saves. Your editor already saves your file; a commit is a claim that a piece of work is complete enough to be recorded, and it should be reserved for that.

There is a legitimate exception worth knowing. Work-in-progress commits on a private branch, made to preserve state before an experiment, are a normal and useful practice. The expectation is that such commits are cleaned up — squashed and given real messages — before the branch is merged. What must not happen is work-in-progress commits reaching main and being left there as the permanent record.

Takeaway: Commit when a change is complete, not when you stop working for the day.

name.text: 15 Content: The Conventional Commits Specification

questiontext.text:
The Conventional Commits Specification

Ad-hoc commit messages degrade predictably. A log of "fixed typos," "more edits," and "updated XML" carries no information that could not be obtained by reading the diffs, which means the log has failed (Huskey, 2024). The remedy adopted in this course is a formal message grammar: the Conventional Commits specification.

The specification mandates a structured subject line (Conventional Commits, n.d.):

<type>[optional scope]: <description>

[optional body]

[optional footer(s)]

The type is drawn from a fixed vocabulary and states the kind of change. The optional scope, in parentheses, states where the change applies. The description states what changed, in the imperative mood and lower case, without a closing period. The body — separated by a blank line — carries the rationale, and the footers carry structured metadata.

The value of a fixed grammar is that it makes the log machine-readable. A history written this way can be filtered, counted, and summarized programmatically: every apparatus correction, every normalization decision, every AI-assisted commit can be extracted with a single command. A history written ad hoc can only be read one line at a time by a human being, which in practice means it is not read at all.

Vocabulary. Type — the fixed-vocabulary term classifying a commit. Scope — an optional parenthesized noun naming the affected component. Footer / trailer — structured Key: value metadata at the end of a commit message.

Takeaway: A fixed message grammar makes the commit log queryable, which is what makes it usable as an apparatus.

name.text: 16 Content: Mapping Commit Types to Editorial Acts

questiontext.text:
Mapping Commit Types to Editorial Acts

Conventional Commits was written for software, and its vocabulary reflects that. This course adopts the specification but binds each type to a specific class of editorial intervention, so that the log describes philological work rather than programming work (Huskey, 2024).

Type Editorial meaning Example
feat New material: a witness, a division, a translation, an apparatus entry feat(collation): add witness N for lines 1-20
fix Correction of an error: a mistranscription, an invalid tag, a wrong siglum fix(apparatus): correct siglum from V to N at line 14
refactor Systemic change to encoding method, with no change to the reading refactor(epidoc): move inline app entries to external div
chore Maintenance: metadata, formatting, normalization passes chore(unicode): normalize Greek text to NFC
docs Editorial documentation: README, method notes, decision records docs(method): record normalization policy for iota subscript
test Validation work: schema checks, error-rate measurement scripts test(schema): add RelaxNG validation for edition.xml

The distinction between fix and refactor is the one that repays attention, because it maps onto a genuine philological difference. A fix changes what the edition claims — the reading was wrong and is now right. A refactor changes how the edition expresses a claim that is unchanged — the same reading, encoded differently. Giarratano's shift from positive to negative apparatus was a refactor of enormous scope, and recording it as such would have marked it as a methodological change rather than a textual one (Huskey, 2024).

Use chore sparingly. It is a genuine category for mechanical maintenance, but it is also the path of least resistance, and a log in which most commits are chore is a log whose author was not thinking about classification.

Takeaway: The type prefix classifies the kind of editorial act, and fix versus refactor marks the difference between changing a claim and changing its expression.

name.text: 17 Content: The Commit Body: Recording Rationale, Not Description

questiontext.text:
The Commit Body: Recording Rationale, Not Description

The subject line says what changed. The body says why — and the body is where the scholarship lives. A diff already shows what changed, exhaustively and without ambiguity; no prose description can improve on it. What the diff cannot supply is the reasoning, and that is irrecoverable once forgotten.

Compare two records of the same edit:

fix(transcription): correct reading at line 14

fix(transcription): correct ἐγένετο to ἐγένοντο at line 14

The plural is required by the compound subject in line 13. Collation
against the facsimile at f. 42v confirms the manuscript reads -οντο;
the singular in my Tuesday transcription was an eye-skip to the
identical form in line 11. Cf. the same error corrected at 2.7.

The first is adequate bookkeeping. The second is a scholarly note: it states the evidence, identifies the cause of the original error, and cross-references a related decision. Six weeks from now, when you are writing the commentary layer and need to explain this reading, the second commit has already written half of it (Huskey, 2024).

The habit to build is to write the body as though for a reader who does not have your current context — because in December, you will be that reader. State what the manuscript shows, what you decided, and what evidence or principle decided it. Where a decision was genuinely uncertain, say so and say what would resolve it; a recorded uncertainty is far more useful to a later editor than a confident silence.

Takeaway: The diff records what you changed; only the commit body can record why, and only if you write it at the time.

name.text: 18 Content: Reading History with `git log`

questiontext.text:
Reading History with `git log`

A log is only valuable if it can be interrogated. git log in its bare form prints commits in reverse chronological order with full metadata, which is rarely the view you want. Its options turn it into a genuine research instrument.

Command Returns Editorial use
git log --oneline One line per commit A rapid overview of the edition's development
git log --oneline --graph The same, with the DAG drawn Seeing where branches diverged and merged
git log --follow <file> History of one file across renames The full record of one transcription
git log -S "ἐγένοντο" Commits that added or removed a string Finding when a reading entered the text
git log --grep="apparatus" Commits whose messages match a pattern Retrieving all apparatus-related decisions
git log --since="2026-10-01" Commits within a date range Reconstructing a week's work for a report

The -S option — the "pickaxe" — deserves particular attention, because it has no analogue in ordinary file management and it answers a question philologists ask constantly: when did this reading enter the text, and who put it there? Given a form you are unsure about, -S returns exactly the commits that introduced or removed it, and the commit body then supplies the rationale.

You will use these in Week 12, when the commentary layer requires you to justify editorial decisions made two months earlier. Students who wrote informative commit bodies retrieve their reasoning in seconds. Students who wrote "updates" reconstruct it from memory, badly.

Takeaway: git log with -S and --grep turns the commit history into a searchable record of editorial decisions.

name.text: 19 Content: Reading Change with `git diff`

questiontext.text:
Reading Change with `git diff`

Where log shows which commits exist, diff shows what they altered. It operates between any two states Git knows about, which includes states you have not committed.

Invocation Compares Answers
git diff Working directory against index What have I changed but not staged?
git diff --staged Index against last commit What exactly am I about to commit?
git diff HEAD Working directory against last commit What have I changed since the last commit?
git diff abc123 def456 Any two commits What changed between these two states?
git diff main..experiment Two branches How does this editorial hypothesis differ?

git diff --staged should become reflexive. It is the last check before a commit becomes permanent, and it catches the two most common errors — staging a file you did not intend to include, and failing to stage one you did.

For a scholarly edition, git diff main..experiment is the powerful case. It renders the full difference between two complete editorial approaches as a structured document — which is, precisely, an apparatus criticus generated automatically from your own work. When in Week 6 you produce a hand-normalized text and a script-normalized text, this command is how you will compare them.

Takeaway: diff compares any two states Git knows about, including two competing editorial hypotheses on separate branches.

name.text: 20 Content: Why the Default Diff Algorithm Fails on TEI XML

questiontext.text:
Why the Default Diff Algorithm Fails on TEI XML

Here the general-purpose tool meets the specialized material, and the fit is poor. Git's default diff uses the Myers algorithm, designed for source code, in which lines are typically long and distinctive. Its assumption is that matching lines between two versions is a good proxy for corresponding content.

TEI XML violates that assumption comprehensively. Marked-up philological text is densely nested and full of short, repetitive closing tags: </w>, </rdg>, </app>, </lem>, each occurring hundreds of times and each identical to every other instance. Presented with two versions, Myers finds enormous numbers of equally valid alignments among these identical lines, and frequently selects one that is minimal in edit distance but meaningless in structure — pairing the closing tag of one apparatus entry with that of an entirely different one (Angleraud et al., 2026).

The output is a diff that is technically correct and practically unreadable: a scattering of additions and deletions spread across a region where one word actually changed. A student reviewing such a diff cannot see what happened, and so stops reviewing diffs. The audit trail is intact and useless — the failure mode Huskey (2024) identifies as the real risk in version-controlled editing, where the record exists but no one can read it.

This matters more than it may appear. Every verification practice in this course — checking an HTR output against your ground truth, reviewing an AI-suggested normalization, auditing a collation — depends on your ability to read a diff of XML. If diffs are illegible, verification degrades into trust.

Takeaway: The default diff algorithm misaligns the repetitive closing tags of TEI XML, producing accurate diffs that no one can read.

name.text: 21 Content: Patience and Histogram Diff

questiontext.text:
Patience and Histogram Diff

The fix is to change algorithms, and Git ships with alternatives designed for exactly this failure.

The patience algorithm inverts Myers' approach. Rather than seeking the minimal edit script over all lines, it first discards every line that appears more than once, computes the longest common subsequence over the unique lines that remain, and only then fills in the gaps between those anchors. Because </app> appears hundreds of times it is ignored as an anchor, while the distinct line containing your actual reading is unique and anchors correctly. The result aligns on meaningful content and keeps structural pairs together.

The histogram algorithm extends patience with a refinement to how it handles lines of low occurrence, and is substantially faster on large files. For TEI work it gives output of comparable quality to patience at better performance, and it is the sensible default for this course.

Set it once, globally:

git config --global diff.algorithm histogram

Do this now, before your first transcription. The setting costs nothing, changes no stored data — diff algorithms affect only how differences are displayed, not what is recorded — and it is the difference between a reviewable edition and an unreviewable one.

Vocabulary. Longest common subsequence — the longest sequence of elements appearing in the same order in two sequences, not necessarily contiguously. Anchor — a uniquely matching line used to align two versions before filling in surrounding differences.

Takeaway: diff.algorithm histogram makes TEI diffs legible by anchoring on unique lines instead of repetitive closing tags.

name.text: 22 Content: Line Endings, `.gitattributes`, and Cross-Platform Collaboration

questiontext.text:
Line Endings, `.gitattributes`, and Cross-Platform Collaboration

A second infrastructural hazard is invisible until it destroys a week's diffs. Operating systems disagree about how to end a line: Windows writes a carriage return followed by a line feed (CRLF), while macOS and Linux write a bare line feed (LF).

The consequence in a mixed-platform class is severe. A student edits one word of a transcription on Windows and commits; their editor rewrites every line ending in the file, and Git — which compares bytes — correctly reports that every line changed. The one-word edit is now invisible inside a diff claiming the entire document was rewritten. Nothing is corrupted, but the audit trail for that commit is destroyed.

The remedy is a .gitattributes file at the repository root, which instructs Git to normalize line endings on commit regardless of the committing platform:

* text=auto eol=lf
*.xml text eol=lf
*.md text eol=lf
*.jpg binary
*.tif binary

Commit this file before anyone else touches the repository, so that normalization applies from the beginning. The binary declarations matter too: they stop Git from attempting line-ending conversion on facsimile images, which would corrupt them outright.

.gitattributes also controls diff behaviour per file type, and you will extend it in Week 8 when the apparatus layer makes XML-aware diffing worth configuring specifically.

Takeaway: * text=auto eol=lf in .gitattributes prevents platform line-ending differences from swamping your diffs.

name.text: 23 Content: Pre-Commit Hooks: Automating Editorial Hygiene

questiontext.text:
Pre-Commit Hooks: Automating Editorial Hygiene

Some requirements are too easy to forget and too consequential to leave to memory. Git's answer is the hook: a script that runs automatically at a defined point in the Git workflow. A pre-commit hook runs immediately before a commit is finalized, and if it exits with a non-zero status the commit is aborted.

For a digital editing repository, two checks belong in that hook. The first is Unicode normalization: a short script using Python's unicodedata library rewrites all staged text into Normalization Form C before the commit proceeds (Python Software Foundation, n.d.). The second is schema validation: the staged XML is checked against the EpiDoc RelaxNG schema, so that a structurally invalid file cannot enter the history at all (EpiDoc Guidelines, 2026; TEI Consortium, 2026).

Hooks live in .git/hooks/ and must be executable. A minimal skeleton:

#!/bin/sh
# .git/hooks/pre-commit
python3 tools/normalize_nfc.py || exit 1
xmllint --noout --relaxng schema/tei-epidoc.rng edition/*.xml || exit 1

Note one consequence of where hooks live: .git/hooks/ is not itself version controlled, so hooks do not travel when a repository is cloned. Keep the scripts in a tracked tools/ directory and install them into .git/hooks/ with a setup script — otherwise your collaborators, and the instructor, will not have the checks you rely on.

Why the second check matters will become clear in Week 8: a malformed XML file breaks every downstream process in the pipeline, and the cost of catching it at commit time is a few seconds, while the cost of discovering it three weeks later is a re-encoding.

Takeaway: A pre-commit hook enforces normalization and schema validity automatically, but hooks are not cloned — install them from a tracked directory.

name.text: 24 Content: Commit Trailers and the Documentation of AI Interventions

questiontext.text:
Commit Trailers and the Documentation of AI Interventions

This course will have you use machine assistance every Friday, and will require you to measure it against your own work. That comparison depends on being able to tell, unambiguously and later, which text a machine produced and which text you produced. Memory will not supply this; the repository must.

Git's mechanism is the trailer: structured Key: value metadata on the final lines of a commit message, which Git parses and can filter on (Conventional Commits, n.d.). Every commit in this course that contains machine-generated or machine-corrected content must carry trailers recording the fact.

feat(transcription): add HTR output for ff. 42r-43v

Transkribus model trained on 8 pages of my own diplomatic transcription
(Week 4 Tuesday ground truth). Uncorrected model output; corrections
follow in a separate commit so that raw CER can be measured against
this state.

AI-Generated: true
Model: Transkribus / Text Titan I
Human-Verified: false
Ground-Truth-Commit: a3f9c21

The Human-Verified: false trailer is the one students most often omit and most need. It marks text that has entered the repository but has not yet been checked — the single most dangerous state for an edition, because unverified machine output is indistinguishable on screen from verified transcription. A later commit flips it to true once you have checked the passage against the facsimile.

The requirement is not bureaucratic. Angleraud et al. (2026) document vision-language models achieving a median character error rate of 1.0% on Greek critical editions while simultaneously producing "catastrophic page-level failures" — fluent, entirely fabricated Greek text with no relation to the image. Output that good on average and that bad occasionally is precisely the kind that must be labelled, because spot-checking will not find the failures.

Takeaway: Every commit containing machine-generated text carries trailers recording the model, and whether a human has verified it.

name.text: 25 Content: Auditing Provenance Programmatically

questiontext.text:
Auditing Provenance Programmatically

Trailers earn their keep when the history is queried rather than read. Because the metadata is structured, the whole repository can be interrogated for the provenance of its contents (Huskey, 2024).

Question Command
Which commits introduced machine-generated text? git log --grep="AI-Generated: true"
What remains unverified by a human? git log --grep="Human-Verified: false"
Which models were used across the term? git log --pretty=format:"%(trailers:key=Model)"
How much of the edition is machine-assisted? git rev-list --all --grep="AI-Generated: true" --count
What did a given model contribute? git log --grep="Model: Transkribus"

The second query is the one to run habitually. It produces a live list of everything in your edition that a machine wrote and you have not yet checked — a work queue that maintains itself, and, at the end of term, a statement of exactly how much of your edition rests on unverified automation.

This capability is the concrete form of the reproducibility argument. A reader of your finished edition can ask what came from where and receive an answer derived from the record rather than from your recollection. Cowen-Breen et al. (2023), describing machine learning applied to premodern Greek, emphasize that the value of such tools in scholarship depends on the scholar's ability to state precisely where the machine's judgement enters — which is exactly what these trailers make possible.

Takeaway: Structured trailers let you query your own edition for what a machine wrote and what you have verified.

name.text: 26 Content: Tags and Semantic Versioning for Published States

questiontext.text:
Tags and Semantic Versioning for Published States

Some states of an edition matter permanently: the version submitted for an assignment, the version reviewed by a peer, the version published at term's end. Commit hashes identify these perfectly but cite terribly — a3f9c21 is not a reference a reader can use. A tag attaches a durable name to a commit.

git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Cataloguing and metadata assignment as submitted, Sep 18"

The -a flag creates an annotated tag, which is a full object in the database carrying its own author, date, and message. Lightweight tags — created without -a — are bare pointers with no metadata, and are not appropriate for anything you intend to cite.

The Library of Digital Latin Texts applies semantic versioning to editions, and this course follows the same scheme (Huskey, 2024):

Component Increments when Editorial meaning
Major (2.0.0) Method or markup changes systemically A different editorial approach to the same text
Minor (1.1.0) Material is added without restructuring New witnesses, apparatus entries, or commentary
Patch (1.0.1) Localized errors are corrected Typographic and encoding fixes only

The payoff is citability with recoverable difference. A reviewer given v1.0.0 and v2.0.0 can run git diff v1.0.0..v2.0.0 and see the complete evolution of your editorial thought between two published states — the precise capacity that Giarratano's five print editions destroyed (Huskey, 2024).

Takeaway: Annotated tags with semantic versions give an edition citable states whose differences remain machine-recoverable.

name.text: 27 Content: Case Study: The Library of Digital Latin Texts

questiontext.text:
Case Study: The Library of Digital Latin Texts

The LDLT, operating under the Digital Latin Library, is the fullest realization of the argument this lesson has been making, and it is worth examining as a model for what your own repository is a small instance of.

The project's foundational commitment is the separation of the edition's data from its presentation. A traditional critical edition fuses the two irretrievably: the apparatus is a set of typographic conventions at the foot of a page, and extracting the underlying scholarly claims from that layout is a manual task. The LDLT instead maintains editions as TEI XML in Git repositories, from which any number of presentations — print, web, machine-readable API — can be generated. The edition is a database; the book is one view of it (Huskey, 2024).

This decoupling makes version control not merely useful but necessary. When the edition is a printed artifact, "the edition" is unambiguous — it is the object on the shelf. When the edition is a repository, identity must be established explicitly, which is what the annotated tag and the semantic version supply. The LDLT requires its editors to use both, so that any state of any edition can be cited and retrieved exactly (Huskey, 2024).

The editorial workflow is correspondingly formalized. Editors work in branches; changes arrive by pull request; review happens on the diff, with reviewers commenting on specific lines of the proposed change. Peer review of an edition thus operates on the change rather than on the finished object — reviewers see not only what the editor concluded but what the editor altered and why. This is the workflow you will practise in the Week 5 reconciliation exercise and in every peer review thereafter.

Takeaway: The LDLT treats an edition as a versioned database with citable releases, making peer review operate on changes rather than on finished objects.

name.text: 28 Content: Case Study: The Perseids Platform and Undergraduate Editing

questiontext.text:
Case Study: The Perseids Platform and Undergraduate Editing

Perseids, developed at Tufts University in association with the Perseus Project, demonstrates that the workflow in this lesson is achievable by undergraduates — which is the relevant question for you this week (Almas & Beaulieu, 2012).

The platform was built to address a specific bottleneck: an enormous stock of inscriptions and manuscripts that had never been transcribed or translated, and a supply of students capable of the work but not of the infrastructure it required. Perseids' response was to keep the scholarly rigour and absorb the infrastructural burden. Underneath, it runs SoSOL, a papyrological editing platform built directly on a Git repository, so that every student intervention is a commit in a real version-controlled history (Almas & Beaulieu, 2012).

Two architectural choices are worth noting for your own work. First, texts are addressed with CTS URNs — canonical identifiers that resolve to specific hierarchical locations in a work, so that urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0012.tlg001. perseus-grc1:1.1 identifies a precise textual node independently of any file or page. Second, transcriptions are linked to high-resolution facsimiles through an open annotation model, so that each editorial claim is anchored to the image evidence supporting it (Almas & Beaulieu, 2012). You will build both of these relations for your own passage: CTS-style identifiers in Week 2, image anchoring in Week 3.

The pedagogical result is the one this course is designed around. Because student work arrives as reviewable commits on branches, the instructor can assess the process — how a transcription developed, what was tried and abandoned, where judgement was exercised — rather than only the final artifact. Your commit history is part of what is being evaluated, and it is evidence of thinking that a finished file cannot supply.

Takeaway: Perseids shows undergraduates producing genuine version-controlled editions, with the commit history itself serving as evidence of scholarly process.

name.text: 29 Content: Interfaces, Accessibility, and Where Effort Should Go

questiontext.text:
Interfaces, Accessibility, and Where Effort Should Go

A caution against a misplaced emphasis. This lesson has used command-line examples throughout, because commands are unambiguous to write down. It does not follow that you must work at the command line.

The command line imposes real costs: syntax memorization, unforgiving error messages, and a cognitive load that competes directly with the philological thinking that is the actual point of the course. Huskey (2024) is explicit that students should be permitted and encouraged to use graphical interfaces and editor integrations for routine staging and committing, on the principle that mental effort should be spent on textual problems rather than on tool syntax.

Interface Best suited to Limitation
Command line Precise operations, scripting, hooks, unusual cases Steep syntax burden; unhelpful errors
VS Code Git integration Staging, committing, diff review during editing Obscures what commands are actually run
Oxygen XML Git support Committing without leaving the XML editor Limited to common operations
GitHub Desktop Visual staging and history browsing Little support for hooks or advanced work

The distinction to hold is between understanding and typing. You are responsible for understanding the object model, the DAG, atomicity, and what a commit records — that is conceptual knowledge, and it is examinable. Whether you produce a commit by typing git commit or by clicking a button in VS Code is a matter of preference, and the resulting commit is byte-identical either way.

Use the interface that leaves you the most attention for the manuscript. Reach for the command line when you need something a graphical tool does not expose — which will happen, particularly with hooks, trailers, and -S searches.

Takeaway: Understand the model conceptually; use whichever interface leaves you the most attention for the philology.

name.text: 30 Content: Synthesis: The Repository as Research Journal

questiontext.text:
Synthesis: The Repository as Research Journal

Everything in this lesson serves one claim, which Huskey (2024) states as the thesis of version-controlled editing: a scholarly edition should be reproducible and explainable, and the repository is the instrument that makes it so.

Reproducible means that any state of the edition can be recovered exactly. The content-addressable object store and the cascading hash chain provide this absolutely — any commit can be checked out and will be byte-identical to the state recorded. Explainable means that any decision can be traced to its rationale. Nothing in Git provides this automatically; it is supplied entirely by atomic commits, informative bodies, and honest trailers. The first property is architectural, the second is a discipline, and only the second can be neglected — which is exactly why it is what this course assesses.

The practices to carry into Week 2 and beyond:

  • Commit atomically — one editorial act per commit, describable without "and".
  • Type every commit with a Conventional Commits prefix that classifies the act.
  • Write bodies that record evidence and reasoning, for the reader you will be in December.
  • Trail every machine-assisted commit with its model and verification status.
  • Tag every submitted state with an annotated semantic version.
  • Configure diff.algorithm histogram and .gitattributes before the first transcription.

Due this week. Choose your manuscript passage by Friday, September 4. The selection is ungraded, but every assignment from Week 2 to Week 13 builds on it, so choose a passage with legible script, at least two available witnesses, and a manageable length — twenty to forty lines. Record the choice and your reasons in your repository's README.md, and commit it.

Takeaway: Reproducibility is guaranteed by Git's architecture; explainability is guaranteed only by your commit discipline, which is why the commit discipline is what is assessed.
